summary: This document defines the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) over HTTPS transport binding and the ipps URI scheme, used to designate the location of a secure IPP print service or a resource it manages.

plainLanguage.summary: Printing over a network can be spied on. This says how to send print jobs through the same secure connection that websites use, with a web address starting ipps.

subtitle: How print clients reach a secure IPP printer over HTTPS, and the ipps:// address scheme that names it.

tldr.problem: Upgrading an IPP connection to TLS within HTTP was implemented unreliably, and some clients and printers only went secure for selected operations, risking exposure of print data.
tldr.mechanism: A client turns an ipps URI into an https URI (using port 631 when none is given), opens an HTTPS connection, and sends IPP requests over it with HTTP POST.
tldr.outcome: IPP gets a secure transport binding and the ipps URI scheme, and IPP clients and printers that support it MUST use TLS 1.2 or higher.

today: RFC 7472 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 2910 and RFC 2911 and sits alongside RFC 3510 as an alternate binding.

sections.title: What This RFC Defines
sections.content:
This RFC defines the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) over HTTPS transport binding and the matching ipps URI scheme. An ipps URI names a secure IPP print service or a network resource it manages. The work came from the IPP Working Group of the IEEE-ISTO Printer Working Group, as part of the PWG IPP Everywhere project for secure mobile printing with vendor-neutral client software.

It is an alternate binding to the original IPP URL scheme in RFC 3510, which it does not update or obsolete. It does update RFC 2910 (encoding and transport) and RFC 2911 (model and semantics) to add the new scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: Printers already had an address style. This adds a new address style for printers that talk through a locked envelope.

sections.title: Why a New Scheme
sections.content: The RFC gives three reasons. First, some existing IPP client and printer implementations of upgrading to TLS within HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2817) are flawed and unreliable, though not because of defects in RFC 2817 itself. Second, some implementations do not upgrade at the start of every HTTP connection and only go secure for selected operations on the same TCP connection, which the RFC calls inherently dangerous. Third, even a printer that demands an upgrade can expose client data if the Expect request header is not used, because the client can send its whole Print-Job request before the printer says it must encrypt first.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way of switching to a secret code partway through was easy to get wrong, and a document could be sent before the switch happened.

sections.title: The HTTPS Transport Binding
sections.content:
When using an ipps URI, an IPP client MUST set up its connection in four steps. It picks an ipps URI, for example from a printer-uri-supported attribute, a directory entry or a web page. It converts that URI to an https URI, replacing ipps with https and inserting the URI's port, or port 631 if none is given. It opens an HTTPS connection to that endpoint. Then it sends requests and receives responses over that connection using the POST method from RFC 7231.

Because the connection is HTTPS from the start, there is no later upgrade step to get wrong.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer swaps the secret-address prefix for the normal secure-website prefix, opens the locked connection first, and only then sends the print job.

sections.title: The ipps URI Scheme
sections.content:
The scheme is defined in ABNF as ipps:// host [ : port ] [ absolute-path [ ? query ] ]. If the port is empty or not given, port 631 MUST be used. This is the same well-known port used for ipp URIs, so one port serves both with or without TLS. If the absolute path is missing, it MUST be given as / when used as a Request-URI. The userinfo component of the generic URI syntax is not allowed.

In IPP exchanges ipps URIs MUST be absolute, and MUST use UTF-8 with percent encoding for octets outside US-ASCII. The abstract protocol limits a URI to 1023 octets, but printers SHOULD NOT generate URIs longer than 255 octets because many older clients do not handle them. Clients SHOULD avoid the query part, since its meaning would be implementation defined. Literal IPv4 or IPv6 addresses SHOULD NOT be used, because addresses change, do not map simply to security domains, are hard to validate against X.509 certificates, and link-local addresses are not portable.

To compare two ipps URIs, clients MUST use the same rules as for http and https in RFC 7230, except that an empty or missing port is treated as equal to port 631.
sections.plainLanguage: An ipps address says which printer to call and, if you like, which door to knock on. If you do not say, it knocks on door 631.

sections.title: Example Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC lists well-formed examples such as ipps://example.com/, ipps://example.com/ipp/print and ipps://example.com:631/ipp/print. Each different path names a logically different IPP Printer, even if they share a host: print might be a load-balancing spooler, while bob and ira might be two physical devices or two queues on one device. The second and third URIs above are equivalent, since port 631 is the default.

Using an explicit ipp path component followed by a service such as print, faxout or scan is described as best practice.
sections.plainLanguage: One building can hold many printers, and the part of the address after the name picks which one you mean.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is motivated by mobile devices printing to enterprise and cloud print services across the public Internet, for example from hotel or airport wireless hotspots. It lists four threats. A faked ipps URI could point to a rogue print service that collects job metadata or documents. An unauthorized client could use a URI to read privacy-sensitive data such as job-originating-user-name. An application layer gateway, such as an IPP to LPD gateway, could silently compromise IPP security, and there is no general client defense, so administrators SHOULD avoid such setups. Finally, an ipps URI carries no parameters for the required client authentication, so clients SHOULD discover it via directories or by reading attributes such as uri-authentication-supported and uri-security-supported with Get-Printer-Attributes.

Server and client authentication in RFC 2910, HTTP/1.1 and TLS 1.2 address the first two threats. Clients and printers that support this specification MUST use TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246) or a higher version for all ipps connections.
sections.plainLanguage: A fake printer could pretend to be the real one, so you should check who you are talking to, and the locked envelope has to be a modern strong one.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has registered the keyword value ipps for the IPP Printer printer-uri-supported attribute, and the ipps URI scheme with status Permanent. The registration notes that the widely deployed open source CUPS print service had supported ipps URIs for several years before this document, and that PWG IPP Everywhere requires them for mandatory data integrity and negotiable data confidentiality. The author and change controller is the IESG.
sections.plainLanguage: The new address prefix was written into the official list of names so nobody else uses it for something different.
